pages.title: Privacy
pages.content:
At Shiosai Resort, we protect the privacy of our guests with straightforward, transparent practices. We only collect the minimal personal information necessary to manage room enquiries, bookings, and seasonal correspondence.

How is guest information collected and processed?

When you contact us to check dates or reserve a room, Rafael Ortiz and Ana Duarte collect your name, email address, telephone number, arrival dates, and specific accommodation preferences. This information is utilized exclusively to generate your 48-hour held offer, process the 20 percent confirmation deposit, and prepare your arrival. We do not sell, rent, or distribute guest information to commercial third parties, advertising brokers, or external online travel booking portals.

How are newsletter addresses and guest records protected?

Subscribers to The Tide Letter have their email addresses held securely for our two seasonal mailings in March and late August. Contact details submitted for general queries or telephone bookings at +00 0000 0000 are archived safely and accessible only to management. You have the right at any time to request a copy of the personal details we hold or to request immediate deletion of your records by writing to stay@shiosai-resort.example.

posts.title: The tide pools at 07:00
posts.excerpt: Kwame Mensah walks the rock pools with whoever is up early, bucket in hand.
posts.content:
At low tide a line of rock pools opens along the north end of the beach, and at 07:00 Kwame Mensah is usually already standing beside the first one. He does not run a lesson. He crouches, points, and lets whoever has come along look for the small crab that lives under the flat stone.

Children who have been told to hurry all year find the pace strange for a minute, and then stop noticing it. The walk ends before breakfast, which starts at 07:00 on the terrace, and everyone returns with wet knees and a story.

posts.title: Why the flag goes up at nine
posts.excerpt: Every summer morning at Shiosai Resort, head lifeguard Aiyana Brooks inspects the shoreline and sets the safety flag that guides family swimming along the Merrow coast.
posts.content:
At six in the morning, the shoreline below Shiosai Resort belongs entirely to the incoming tide and the coastal gulls. Along our four hundred metres of sand at Port Merrow, the morning begins well before the first family steps down from the terrace. At half past six, the sand is raked clean of drift kelp, leaving smooth wet ridges where the overnight tide receded. By seven, the aroma of fresh coffee and warm bread drifts from the terrace kitchen as breakfast service opens, and guests begin gathering on their private sea-facing balconies to watch the pale light settle over the water. Yet down on the sand, the water remains quiet and unwatched until exactly nine o'clock.

The routine of the beach belongs to head lifeguard Aiyana Brooks and her team of four certified water safety specialists. Stationed at the white timber tower at the centre of our shoreline, Aiyana begins her inspection at eight o'clock, walking the entire length of the four hundred metres. She reads the shoreline with practiced calm, observing the drift of sandbars, checking the morning swell, and noting where shallow gullies have formed overnight. Because low tide moves about fifty minutes later each day, the shape of the beach is never quite the same as yesterday. Aiyana records the sea temperature, logs the depth of the morning tide pools, and delivers the daily beach report to reception before nine.

At nine o'clock sharp, the green flag rises on the central mast. The raising of the flag is not a ceremonial flourish; it is our clear daily declaration that the beach is staffed, the lookouts are alert, and the shallows are safe for family swimming. Simultaneously, Kwame Mensah opens the kids club under the striped awning on the sand, where children gather with buckets and spades to start building fortress walls before the morning swim lessons. For parents finishing breakfast on the terrace railings above, the green flag against the pale sky is the signal that children may run down the timber boardwalk directly onto the open beach.

Throughout the day between 09:00 and 18:00, from 1 June to 15 September, Aiyana and her team maintain continuous watch over the water. The flag changes whenever coastal conditions shift. If a stiff offshore wind picks up or tidal currents strengthen along the outer sandbanks, the team lowers the green cloth and raises the yellow flag, indicating that swimmers must stay strictly between the marked flag zones and close to shore. On rare days of heavy sea swell, the red flag commands that all swimming ceases. At ten in the morning and again at three in the afternoon, the guards enter the water themselves, coaching children through structured swimming lessons in the sheltered shallows.

When eighteen hundred hours arrives, Aiyana walks the tideline once more, lowers the flag, and secures the watchtower for the evening. As the guards sign off, evening dinner begins on the terrace above, where families gather over Lena Vogt's evening dishes while dusk settles across the Merrow coast. The flag is down, but the water continues its slow rhythm under the evening light, waiting for nine o'clock tomorrow when the green marker will rise again.

posts.title: A Saturday-to-Saturday week
posts.excerpt: One family's summer week, from the Saturday key card to the Saturday suitcase.
posts.content:
Saturday: the key card, the bucket set from the room, the first swim before dinner. Sunday to Friday follow the same easy shape, with lessons at 10:00, the kids' club until 16:00 and dinner on the terrace at six.

By the second Saturday the children know the lifeguards by name. That is the week we sell, and it is the one we plan the rest of the year around.
